body.heading: Set up the race
paragraphs: Put one ice cube on a plate in the sunshine and one on a plate in the shade. Start them at the same time. Which one will melt first?
Ice melts when warmth reaches it. Sunshine carries warmth, so the sunny cube has a head start in the race.

body.heading: Watch and time
paragraphs: Check your cubes every few minutes. The sunny cube shrinks and sits in a growing puddle. The shady cube keeps its shape for longer.
Ask your adult to time how long each cube takes to melt completely. Write the times down — that is real experiment data.

body.heading: Try more racers
paragraphs: Race more cubes in new places: one wrapped in a cloth, one in a bowl of cold water, one with salt sprinkled on it by your adult.
The wrapped cube melts slowly because the cloth keeps warmth out. Salt makes ice melt faster — that is why it is spread on icy winter paths.

takeaway: Ice melts fastest where the most warmth reaches it, and racing cubes in different places proves it.
safetyNotes: An adult should get the ice out of the freezer. Wipe up melted water so nobody slips.
screenFreeExtension: Guess which will dry first — a wet flannel in the sun or in the shade — then test your guess.
